commit.message: docs: add release note for the local reputation subsystem

reputation: benchmark forward cost across many channels

The existing benchmarks drive a single channel pair, so the channel map
and the HTLC index hold one entry. Add a variant that spreads forwards
over 10, 100 and 1000 channels with random pairs so the per-HTLC cost
can be checked against a populated node. The cost stays flat at roughly
0.7us and 13 allocations per forward plus resolve.

itest: test the local reputation subsystem end-to-end

Add an integration test asserting that a forwarding node running the log-only
reputation subsystem forwards, fails and restarts exactly as it would without
it, while emitting the expected reputation log lines.

htlcswitch+lnd: connect reputation manager to the switch

Feed forwarded HTLCs to the reputation subsystem through a read-only seam on
the switch. The switch calls OnForward/OnSettle/OnFail at the circuit layer
behind a nil check, so the subsystem is skipped entirely when disabled. The
manager is wrapped in a panic boundary before being handed to the switch: a
bug in the (log-only) subsystem can never take down HTLC forwarding.

Only the outgoing channel is reported to the subsystem, not an outgoing
circuit key: at forward time the switch has not yet handed the packet to the
outgoing link, so no outgoing HTLC ID exists yet.

The subsystem is enabled by default and can be disabled with the new
routing.no-reputation flag.

Includes unit tests for the switch seam: each hook fires once with the right
keys, a nil manager is a no-op, local sends are skipped, a hook panic is
absorbed by the guard, and a non-strict forward reports the channel the HTLC
actually went out on for both the add and its resolution.

reputation: add the reputation manager

Add the Manager that ties the scoring together behind the OnForward/OnSettle/
OnFail hooks. The hooks run synchronously under a single lock: OnForward
records the pending HTLC and computes (and logs) the reputation decision, both
for the HTLC in isolation and against the risk already in flight on its
outgoing channel, while OnSettle/OnFail resolve it and update the outgoing
reputation and incoming revenue averages. The subsystem is log-only and holds
no persisted state, so reputation re-accrues from live traffic after a restart.

Every resolution drops its own pending HTLC, so a pending that outlives the
worst case time it could be held for means a resolution was never reported to
us. A periodic check warns about those and deliberately leaves them in place
rather than sweeping them away, so the underlying bug stays visible.

Includes unit tests and benchmarks for the per-forward hook cost.

bolt12handler: add BOLT 12 invoice generation

Build a signed BOLT 12 invoice from a validated invoice request: mirror
the request fields, compute the amount, construct the blinded payment
paths carrying the path_id, and sign the Merkle root. An optional
PaymentPathBuilder supplies multi-hop paths. A single-hop path is the
fallback when there is no builder or the builder fails.

The invoice is signed under the node identity key, so an offer without
offer_issuer_id is refused for now.

The package logs under the B12H sub logger.

commit.message:
scripts: check release notes consistency in CI

The release note fragments in docs/release-notes/unreleased are only
consistent as long as the fragments are deleted once their change is
released, and a release is only cut after its fragments were folded into
its release note document. Nothing enforced either, so a forgotten step
would either announce a change twice or ship a release with incomplete
notes.

Add check-release-notes-consistency.sh with two modes. On pull requests, it
fails if a fragment belongs to a PR that is already announced in a
version-wide release note document, which catches both the fold and the
port of a patch release's notes to master. If the pull request bumps
build/version.go to a release version, release candidate or final, it also
requires the release note document of that version to exist and all
fragments to be folded into it. A final release additionally requires a
non-empty contributors section. The release mode runs the same readiness
check in the release build against the tagged commit.

The check runs in its own CI job that ignores the no-changelog label, since
the pull requests that fold fragments or bump the version carry that label.
Release branches keep their release version between releases, so the
readiness check only runs for the pull request that changes the version.

commit.message:
scripts: validate release note fragments in CI

The release note check only verified that the PR's link shows up somewhere
under docs/release-notes, so a fragment with the wrong filename, a missing
link or misspelled headings passed. Since the fragments are consolidated at
release time, such mistakes would only surface then.

Validate every file that a PR adds or modifies in a subdirectory of the
release notes against its base: it must live in unreleased/, start with a
top-level heading and only use the headings of the template or of the
newest version-wide release note document, without the document title or a
contributors section. A newly added fragment must additionally be named
after the PR and link to it. Modified fragments are exempt from that, so
that a follow-up PR can extend the entry of an earlier one.

The existing recursive link check is kept so that version-wide release note
files of older release lines continue to pass. The CI checkout now fetches
two commits so that the base of the PR's merge commit is available.

commit.message:
docs: add per-PR release note fragments

Every PR currently edits the release note document of the next release and
its shared contributor list, so concurrent PRs keep conflicting on the same
lines. Following Bitcoin Core's release note process, new entries are
instead added as one fragment file per PR in docs/release-notes/unreleased.

The fragments are not tied to a release. Each one is folded into the release
note document of the first release that ships the change when that release
is prepared, and the contributor list is generated from Git history. This
means a contributor doesn't need to know whether the change will be
backported: the automated backport workflow cherry-picks the fragment along
with the change, so a backported fix ends up in the next patch release, and
the port of the patch release notes to master deletes the released
fragments there.

The existing release-notes-0.22.0.md and release-notes-0.21.5.md stay as the
baseline for the entries written before this change.

The guide lives in docs/release-notes/README.md. The pull request template,
contribution guidelines, backport workflow documentation and release note CI
failure message point contributors at it.

commit.message:
htlcswitch+peer: cover the close paths the resolution relies on

In this commit, we pin the last contract the resolution of a close rests on
and that nothing yet exercises: the order in which an observer reports and
claims a caller. The preceding commit covers the rest, since a test of the
channel a request derives needs the promise that commit introduces. The
observer must take the caller's record before it reports, so that a closer
which was already retired cannot tell a caller the close succeeded after the
caller was told it had ended. The test drives a real RBF closer to its
terminal state through production code and asserts both outcomes: an unclaimed
caller is told the close succeeded, and a caller a retirement already answered
is not told twice. Removing the claim from the report makes the second case
fail, which is what the ordering is for.

The closer is subscribed to before it is driven, since registering the
subscription inside the observer goroutine races the event that drives it, so
a state reached in between would be missed and the observer would wait for a
transition that already happened.

Two more paths are covered, both of which decide whether a caller is answered:
a close that ends in a breach, and a caller whose record is given up while
another caller on the channel is still waiting. The tests for a close reported
after the peer shut down state what they rely on and the one schedule they do
not catch.

htlcswitch: resolve a close request once, without blocking

In this commit, we give a cooperative close request a single outcome that
every path can resolve at most once, and that no path can be held up
delivering.

The request carried its error over a channel with room for one, and the
paths that end a close wrote to it directly. Two of those writes have no way
out if the buffer is already full: they send without selecting on anything
else, so once the caller has stopped reading they block where they stand. One
of them runs on the channel manager's goroutine, so a block there stops every
operation for that peer, not just the close. The preceding commit makes the
disconnect path answer a waiting caller, adding a second writer to a request
that previously had one, so the buffer may already hold an outcome when either
send runs.

The request now carries a promise instead of a channel. Completion is
idempotent and reports whether this call was the one that resolved it, so a
second path is refused rather than allowed to overwrite the outcome the
caller already has. Completion cannot block, so a path that resolves a close
is never held up by a caller that stopped reading.

A close that reaches its close resolves the request too, once the caller has
been told it succeeded. Otherwise the request is resolved only when a close
fails or is aborted, and a caller that derived a channel from it has nothing
to end that wait: with a context that is never cancelled, as the breach path
uses, that wait would outlive everything it was waiting for.

Callers that wait on a channel see no change: the promise is awaited on their
behalf, and only a failure is forwarded, since a close that succeeds reports
through its updates. The channel is left open rather than closed, because a
closed channel reads as an immediate nil error and would cut a wait short
before the close had finished.

Retiring a closer no longer writes to the channel it is retiring. Clearing the
channel's closing flag happens only where the goroutine that owns the channel
does it, which the channel manager also does for its own channels as it
drains, so no request carries the channel and no resolution touches one.

The updates a close emits keep their untyped channel, because their terminal
value carries a chancloser type and chancloser imports this package. Every
send is guarded so that a caller that has gone away cannot make a close block
delivering to it, and the buffer holds a pending update from each side of the
negotiation as well as the terminal one.

The failure and success of a close are reported by name. A close that failed
takes the caller's own record before reporting, so a close that afterwards
reached its close cannot tell that caller it succeeded: resolving a request
refuses a second resolution, but the updates a close carries are a separate
channel that nothing refuses.

A close that reached its close reports to every caller still waiting, and the
peer's shutdown no longer suppresses that report. The closing transaction has
been broadcast, so it confirms whether or not the peer is still connected, and
the callers' records are taken before anything is delivered, so no other path
could answer them.

The error a confirmation reports is reported through a callback rather than a
channel, so there is no relay goroutine that a peer shutdown could stop before
it forwards the error.

A close refused because the counterparty breached the channel resolves its
request, and the request that path starts is bound to the daemon's lifetime,
so a request nothing resolves cannot outlive the daemon.
